query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under simultaneous sliding wear and corrosive attack at elevated temperature, the multi-phase eutectic structure forms local galvanic couples at phase boundaries, which, when coupled with repeated oxide film rupture by mechanical wear, accelerates both metal dissolution and mechanical material removal beyond the sum of their separate effects.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA with distinct phases featuring varying electrochemical potentials (e.g., FCC and intermetallic σ-phase) in an as-cast or as-clad condition and free of prior tribocorrosion damage.
generation.intervention: Apply a combined tribological load (e.g., pin-on-disk) under a corrosive environment at elevated temperature, ensuring controlled normal load, sliding speed, solution composition, and temperature.
generation.conditions: Test temperatures near the alloy’s intended high-temperature service regime, using an electrolyte solution that promotes pitting/galvanic corrosion (e.g., a chloride-containing solution). Compare to identical specimens tested separately under (a) only mechanical wear (no solution) and (b) only corrosion (no mechanical contact).
generation.structural_mediator: Local galvanic activity between eutectic phases and repeated disruption of oxide films along phase boundaries, exposing underlying material to continuous oxidation and dissolution.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical rubbing disrupts the protective oxide layer and induces microcracks. The ensuing repeated exposure of fresh metal surfaces fosters galvanic interactions where one phase selectively dissolves, aggravating corrosion and weakening the material. The resulting damage accelerates wear under load, amplifying total material loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: Total material loss under simultaneous wear-corrosion conditions rises beyond the sum of losses due to wear alone and corrosion alone. Both wear rate and corrosion rate are expected to increase compared to their independent values, with severe local attack at phase boundaries.
generation.baseline: Wear-only and corrosion-only tests on matching alloy specimens under the same mechanical and environmental parameters (load, temperature, solution, etc.) examined in isolation.
generation.boundary: Elevated temperatures near or slightly beyond the alloy’s oxidative stability range, in media that can disrupt oxide films or induce galvanic currents. If the alloy has less pronounced phase contrast or if the environment is minimally corrosive, synergy may be less pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: Exact magnitude of synergy cannot be definitively predicted without direct measurement. Additional unaccounted factors (e.g., tribofilm formation, local temperature spikes) may alter outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct tribocorrosion tests on statistically identical multi-phase eutectic HEA specimens under three conditions: (1) corrosion-only (no mechanical wear), (2) wear-only (no corrosive electrolyte), and (3) simultaneous tribocorrosion at the same temperature and nominal stress levels. Compare total mass loss and surface damage with that predicted by summing (1) and (2).
measurements: In situ monitoring of friction coefficients during wear
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., current density) during corrosion
Surface analysis (SEM/EDS) for microstructural damage contributions from wear vs. corrosion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined tribocorrosion condition does not produce a statistically higher total degradation than the sum of separate wear and corrosion trials (within experimental error), the hypothesized synergistic effect is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In order to prepare coating with good friction and wear resistance at elevated temperature on the surface of hot-working tool steel, by using a CO2 laser, FeCrNiTiZr high-entropy alloy coating with different laser scanning speeds (360, 480 and 600 mm/min, respectively) was successfully fabricated by using laser cladding technology on the surface of H13 steel in this paper. Phase constitutions, microhardness, microstructure, and wear characteristics of FeCrNiTiZr coatings under different laser scanning speeds were analyzed. It was determined that 480 mm/min was the optimal laser scanning speed. The results showed that the coating at the scanning speed of 480 mm/min consists of a BCC phase with significant lattice distortion and high dislocation density; the crystal structure is cellular crystal and dendrite crystal. The coating demonstrates the highest microhardness (842 HV0.2), which is 4.2 times that of the substrate (200 HV0.2). Its average friction coefficients at room temperature and 823 K are approximately one-seventh and one-third of the substrate’s, respectively, and its wear volume is reduced by about 98% and 81% under these conditions. AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power

occupying_moves.lever: simultaneous mechanical loading and corrosive environment under elevated temperature
occupying_moves.technique: high-temperature tribocorrosion tests (pin-on-disk or similar) with in-situ electrochemical monitoring and post-test microstructural/chemical analysis (SEM/EDS, XRD)
occupying_moves.conditions: multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy, controlled sliding speed, normal load, temperature, and corrosive medium composition

chosen.lever: simultaneous mechanical loading and corrosive environment under elevated temperature
chosen.technique: high-temperature tribocorrosion tests (pin-on-disk or similar) with in-situ electrochemical monitoring and post-test surface characterization
chosen.conditions: multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy, varying normal load, sliding speed, temperature (up to intended operating conditions), and electrolyte aggressiveness
chosen.why: A controlled-variable tribocorrosion experiment in elevated-temperature corrosive conditions provides a direct way to isolate and quantify the synergy between oxidation/corrosion and wear. By carefully tuning normal load, sliding speed, and temperature, researchers can track how mechanical damage promotes oxide-film breakdown, intensifies local galvanic activity in the multi-phase structure, and thus accelerates total degradation. Standard tribological and electrochemical methods can measure wear rates, corrosion current density, and material loss, offering a clear test of the proposed mechanism and a means to falsify it if such synergistic acceleration does not match the predicted changes in both separate (wear and corrosion) and combined degradation rates.
